abstract: Boreal forests were commonly known to be limited in their productivity by low temperatures and low nitrogen (N) availability. Recently, evidence has accumulated that an increasing boreal forest area has switched from temperature limitation to drought limitation. Co-limitation by N in drought-limited boreal forests is hardly studied. Therefore, the Dry Boreal Forest Long-Term Nitrogen Fertilization Experiment (DryBoreal-LTNE) has been set up in drought-limited southern boreal forest of Mongolia, where natural mature forests of Larix sibirica are fertilized with 0, 6.25, 12.5, and 25 kg N ha-1 a-1 in an area that is thought to received ca. 1-2 kg N ha-1 a-1 from atmospheric deposition. In the second year of fertilization, we analyzed non-structural hydrate concentrations (NSC) in foliage, stem phloem and branch and stem xylem. Concentrations of soluble sugars in foliage and young distal branches increased with increasing doses of N fertilization, pointing to a strong limitation of photosynthesis by low ambient N supply. By contrast, NSC concentrations in old branches, stem sapwood and heartwood, which are plant parts for long-term NSC storage, decreased especially due to low N fertilization. This finding indicates the mobilization of NSC for supporting increased N uptake, increased synthesis of chlorophylls and proteins, and eventually growth. Conversely, it suggests that NSC were partly allocated to the wood, because N limited the use of assimilates for metabolite synthesis.
